question: The marmot is a protected species under the Bern Convention, which was ratified by the European Union by means of a Council decision of 3 December 1981. As a result, the EU must put in place measures to prohibit ‘the use of all indiscriminate means of capture and killing’ (Article 8) which may cause marmots to disappear, unless they cause significant damage to crops and livestock in particular.

Although scientists have noted a continuous decline in the French marmot population since the 1990s – the species is threatened by multiple factors (land take, habitat destruction and climate degradation in particular) – marmots are still being hunted in around ten French departments.
However, there is no serious evidence or official data demonstrating that marmot populations are multiplying and causing damage that could justify hunting the animal. 1.
What measures has the European Commission put in place to ensure that the Member States, in particular France, are complying with the Bern Convention?
Does the Commission intend to strengthen the protection of marmots by means of additional measures or by generalising the ban on hunting marmots in the EU?
answer: 1. Contracting Parties to the Bern Convention are under an obligation to keep the populations of species listed in its Appendix III out of danger and to put in place appropriate measures to address the main threats to the specie s (1). At EU level, only the marmot subspecies Marmota marmota latirostris, is listed in Annex IV of the Habitats Directive (2).

Accordingly, only this subspecies is strictly protected under the directive. Deliberate killing of this subspecies in the wild, including hunting, is prohibited in the EU. The other subspecies, including those to which the French populations belong, are not listed in the Habitats Directive. 2.

In any case, the establishment and implementation of such measures for the species Marmota marmota also lies with the individual Member States, who are Parties to the Convention. France is therefore under the obligation to enact measures to protect the alpine marmot and to ban hunting practices under national law, as appropriate.

Articles 2 and 7 of the Bern Convention: https://www.coe.int/en/web/conventions/full-list?module=treaty-detail&treatynum=104 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7-50.
